questions.problem: Let $I=[0,1]⊂R$ and ${X}_{i}=[0,i]\times [0,1].$ Which of the following represents ${⋂}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the intersection of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *all* the sets:

$$
{⋂}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}=\{x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for all}\,\,k\in I\}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=0.5,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{0.5}=[0,0.5]\times [0,1]=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in [0,0.5],b\in [0,1]\}.
$$

This represents a rectangle whose vertices are at $(0,0),$ $(0.5,0),$ $(0.5,1),$ and $(0,1)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14130949/assets/5b882f3fb0e7b44eb2df3a510260574e5c4a4d85842a9c0d65515f1a40894756.png)

In general,

$$
{X}_{i}=[0,i]\times [0,1]=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in [0,i],b\in [0,1]\}
$$

is the rectangle whose vertices are at $(0,0),$ $(i,0),$ $(i,1),$ and $(0,1).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14130949/assets/cb530698591dbd71a8058d9faa0c60b636dc654f21e92d65ec8295aeaa67355a.png)

The intersection of all these rectangles is the line segment $\{0\}\times [0,1]:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14130949/assets/704f8f6f0666d09bb2b8a25eab0548c3eb808e2c9d394d2ae873de35cb0112d1.png)

questions.problem: Which of the following is a representation of the set $S={Z}^{-}\times N$ in the Cartesian plane?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S={Z}^{-}\times N
$$

contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is a negative integer and whose $y$-coordinate is a natural number.

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in {Z}^{-},\,y\in N\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider ${S}_{-1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $-1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any natural number.

$$
{S}_{-1}=\{(-1,y)\,:\,y\in N\}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{-1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14130949/assets/8e6816767cd2010fca1b8991ed9c5e0c42d3a6d6466d78025534bc8362a174b9.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{-2}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $-2$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any natural number.

$$
{S}_{-2}=\{(-2,y)\,:\,y\in N\}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{-2}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14130949/assets/4d0fe261e790520e6a8786e6f024d5b9cb7cd54c18242103a1f4b77f09653abc.png)

We can create the subsets $…,{S}_{-5},{S}_{-4},{S}_{-3}$ similarly. Our Cartesian product $S$ is the *union* of these subsets:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =…{S}_{-4}\cup {S}_{-3}\cup {S}_{-2}\cup {S}_{-1} \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in {Z}^{-}}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize ${Z}^{-}\times N$ as the set of points in the diagram below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14130949/assets/f7e54dd973126e3179e79b1ba1a26f4a7c1c541ca764b14c4ccef73b4452509e.png)

questions.problem: Which of the following represents the set $S=[-1,1]\times [0,1]$ in the Cartesian plane?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian product $A\times B$ consists of all ordered pairs whose first coordinate belongs to $A$ and whose second coordinate belongs to $B.$

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set

$$
S=[-1,1]\times [0,1]
$$

contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in [-1,1],\,y\in [0,1]\}.
$$

To visualize $S$, consider ${S}_{0}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $0$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
{S}_{0}=\{(0,y)\,:\,y\in [0,1]\}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{0}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14130949/assets/1cc30fcc7543bfbbf8c5c59d1436eb3b1a0799d60c9ad1d899957e8fd17d58ab.png)

Now, consider a general ${S}_{i}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals some $i\in [-1,1]$ and whose $y$-coordinate is any real number in the interval $[0,1].$

$$
{S}_{i}=\{(i,y)\,:\,y\in [0,1]\}
$$

For each $i\in [-1,1],$ ${S}_{i}$ is a vertical line segment from the point $(i,0)$ to the point $(i,1).$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14130949/assets/494c9d77b0ff339b90792270c9d641054a03a2918e3c56a93747b42a77ee3ccf.png)

Our Cartesian product $S$ is the union of these subsets over $I=[-1,1]:$

$$
S={⋃}_{i\in I}{S}_{i}.
$$

As $i$ runs over $I,$ these line segments sweep the following rectangle that represents the union ${⋃}_{i\in I}{S}_{i}:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14130949/assets/7c5ac5dad0aaacb4347c260d634e6bcd2d6102b25d51813fe106803417cc7539.png)

$$
A\times B=\{(a,b)\,:\,a\in A,\,b\in B\}
$$

In this case, the set 

$$
S=Z\times [-1,0]
$$

 
contains every point in ${R}^{2}$ whose $x$-coordinate is a integer number and whose $y$-coordinate belongs to $[-1,0].$

$$
S=\{(x,y)\,:\,x\in Z,\,y\in [-1,0]\}
$$

To visualize $S,$ consider ${S}_{-1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $-1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is in $[-1,0].$

$$
{S}_{-1}=\{(-1,y)\,:\,y\in [-1,0]\}
$$

We can represent ${S}_{-1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14130949/assets/63199d9f35c331339e97ad3b2094a520d1fb6a9892bd0beac83538c43b9e2748.png)

Next, consider ${S}_{1}⊂S$ containing all points whose $x$-coordinate equals $1$ and whose $y$-coordinate is in $[-1,0].$

$$
{S}_{1}=\{(1,y)\,:\,y\in R\}.
$$

We can represent ${S}_{1}$ in the plane as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14130949/assets/03a6a90b3eff572ceed341de55a0d5e625e338ca18f2ae8ee85eed3bb5278167.png)

$$
\begin{aligned}R\times N & =…{S}_{-2}\cup {S}_{-1}\cup {S}_{0}\cup {S}_{1}\cup {S}_{2}… \\  & ={⋃}_{i\in Z}{S}_{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can visualize $Z\times [-1,0]$ as the set of vertical lines shown in the diagram below.
